 Clarins brings Emma Roberts and Christina Ricci to 200-guest Austin rooftop
 Clarins gathered 200 guests, including Emma Roberts and Christina Ricci, for an Austin rooftop event spotlighting Double Serum Eye.
 Zoe Park 
 26 Oct 2026 
 • 5 min read 
 ✦

 ↓ 
 Formula 1 weekend brings its own celebrity circuit to Austin. But at one rooftop gathering, the centerpiece was not a race car or a runway. It was a skincare product projected at architectural scale, surrounded by golden light, with actors Emma Roberts and Christina Ricci among the guests.
 French skincare house Clarins used that setting to give Double Serum and Double Serum Eye an entertainment-world moment. Its October 25 announcement described a celebration at The Modern in Austin where a beauty routine became a room people could walk through, photograph and talk about.
 Table of contents
 Jump to each section:
 Why Clarins made the rooftop a product world 
 What Emma Roberts and Christina Ricci brought to the night 
 From Paris Fashion Week to Austin race weekend 
 What beauty marketers can learn from these gatherings 
 Why Clarins made the rooftop a product world
 A serum bottle is usually something a shopper sees at arm's length, while deciding whether the texture, ingredients or price feel right. Clarins changed the scale of that encounter for its Austin event. At The Modern's rooftop, golden lighting, large product projections and installations borrowed from the visual identity of Double Serum made the product an environment rather than a counter display.
 Guests also encountered the brand's longevity messaging through food. Chef Phillip Frankland Lee, founder of Scratch Kitchen, prepared an omakase-style tasting inspired by ingredients associated with the skincare brand's approach. The dinner and lighting were not clinical demonstrations. They translated a product story into different sensory experiences.
 200 guests attended the Austin event, according to Clarins USA. The figure is an event attendance claim, not an estimate of reach or product sales.
 That distinction matters. The staging supplied many things worth photographing, but the guest count alone does not tell us whether attendees later bought Double Serum Eye. It does explain the immediate creative proposition: put a highly technical skincare story into a format that is easy to experience without reading a list of active ingredients.

 The guest list moved between beauty, entertainment and sport. Emma Roberts and Christina Ricci attended, alongside actor Damson Idris, Gavin Casalegno, Carlacia Grant and other guests. These were confirmed attendees at the celebration, not people Clarins announced as new ambassadors.
 There was also an opportunity for the event to live outside the rooftop. Who What Wear shared an Instagram interview with Roberts from the gathering, describing the occasion as Clarins USA's F1 celebration in Austin. The clip made room for a conversation about the actress and her television work rather than simply repeating a skincare product claim.
 View this post on Instagram 
 For viewers who recognize Roberts from Scream Queens or American Horror Story , an entertainment interview is a familiar way into the scene. The brand sits in the background of a piece of celebrity coverage people might have watched for other reasons. That is different from claiming Roberts endorsed the serum, and Clarins has not reported that this appearance produced sales.
 From Paris Fashion Week to Austin race weekend
 The Austin gathering was not an isolated product celebration. Earlier in October, during Paris Fashion Week, Clarins hosted a smaller dinner at KONG to introduce the new generation of Double Serum Eye. The guest mix there included model and creator Nara Smith, Kelly Piquet and guests from fashion and entertainment, according to Clarins' October 1 release .
 Approximately 50 guests attended the Paris dinner, Clarins reported, compared with 200 at the later Austin rooftop gathering.
 The two evenings shared a recognizable pattern without copying one venue's atmosphere into another. Paris used a seated dinner at a fashion-week destination. Austin stretched the same skincare idea into a rooftop light show during a weekend with a strong entertainment presence. In both cases, the setting gave the product a social occasion to inhabit.
 There is a wider beauty-marketing parallel here. YSL Beauty's New York Block Party put makeup and fragrance into the existing nightlife character of La Esquina rather than building a standard department-store experience. Clarins' approach is more tightly attached to a product-science story, but both use a place with cultural meaning to make beauty something guests can encounter socially.
 Clarins says Double Serum Eye combines six plant extracts and five active molecules in a dual-phase formula. Those are product specifications and company-reported benefits, not independently verified performance results from the event. The creative challenge is making such a dense message tangible without pretending a party can prove an efficacy claim.
 What beauty marketers can learn from these gatherings
 For people outside the beauty industry, the appeal of a night like this is simple: the room looks interesting, familiar actors turn up, and the product becomes part of the atmosphere. For marketers, the more important question is how that attention connects back to the brand.
 Give the product a visual role. The Austin projections and gold installations were recognizably tied to Double Serum. A dramatic venue works harder when guests can still tell which product the night is about.
 Let celebrity coverage be more than a scripted endorsement. The Roberts interview offered an example of adjacent entertainment content reaching beyond the product conversation. But an appearance at an event should never be reported as an ambassador agreement without evidence.
 Change the setting without losing the core idea. The Paris dinner and Austin rooftop gave Double Serum Eye different cultural backdrops. The consistent product narrative mattered more than replicating one event format exactly.
 This kind of experiential beauty marketing has a natural measurement problem. Guest lists, event photography and social videos are visible immediately, while consideration and purchases are harder to observe from outside. Clarins has not disclosed attributable sales, conversions or campaign reach for the Austin gathering, so its commercial impact remains unknown.
 The Austin event is nevertheless useful to watch for its creative construction. Rather than make a serum compete for attention in a crowded feed through product claims alone, Clarins built a setting where beauty, nightlife and familiar entertainment figures overlapped. The resulting story is about a product, but also about the cultural occasions a product is invited into.
